# dsh-confirm-gate

> **Stops your AI agent before it rewrites 20 files and burns a day of budget.**
>
> Install it and

every action the model takes is counted. As the budget runs down it
> starts telling the model to br

ake; at the hard limit the model stops and waits for you
> to type `confirm`. **No kernel changes, n
o required config.**
English | 中文 · **v0.3.0**
## What's new in v0.3.0

The gate now stays active under sandbox modes too. Previously it stepped aside in
`read-only` and `w

orkspace-write`, on the reasoning that a sandbox already bounds what
the model can do. That reasonin

g covered *what* the model can touch, not *how many times*
it touches it: 40 file edits inside a wor

kspace-write session are still 40 edits, and
still worth a nudge before the 41st.

So `SANDBOX_MANAGED_MODES` is now empty and the counter runs in every mode. The
counter, the three r

eminder tiers, and the `confirm` release are all unchanged. If you
relied on the old stepping-aside

behaviour, set `SANDBOX_MANAGED_MODES` back to
`['read-only', 'workspace-write']` in `lib/index.js`.

Correctness fix only: the streaming
mode-detection path now reads the mode on each call rather than

caching it, so switching
permission modes mid-session follows immediately.
## What it looks like while running
[代码示例省略，未执行]
**It is not an interceptor; it is a counter that talks.** Every counted call comes with a message. T

he first 10 nudge the model to ask you;
11–14 escalate to an instruction to stop; only the 15th actu

ally blocks the tool.
That gap is what lets the model come to a halt while you are away from the key

locks the tool.
That gap is what lets the model come to a halt while you are away from the keyboard.
## What it saves you
| Situation | Without it | With it |
| The model loops, rewriting the same file | Burns the whole budget | Warns from the 11th call, stop

s at the 15th |
| You step away for half an hour | You come back to 200 changed files | It stopped b

efore you got back |
| You want it to continue | No idea how far it got | Reply `confirm` and the wh
ole turn is released |

**This is not a security sandbox** — sandboxing is DSH's own job. This manages **cost and
direction*
*: it gives the model the ability to brake before it burns money or drifts.
### Trade-offs & known limitations
Listed first, because they are the interesting part.
1. **The first N operations have no gate at all.** In the default `freeLimit: 10` configuration, ope
rations 1–10 are allowed with only a reminder. That window is deliberate — it gives the model room t
o correct itself before being asked to stop. Set `freeLimit: 0` when you want zero tolerance; the pl

ugin then ask-confirms before the very first persistent operation.
2. **`confirm` defends against ac
cidents, not injection.** The threat model is a *trusted user with a fallible model*, where the fail
ure to prevent is unbounded trial-and-error. Prompt injection is a different layer — that is what DS
H's approval channel and sandbox are for. Do not deploy this as the only thing between an untrusted

input and your filesystem.
3. **The release rule is deliberately coarse.** Any message containing th
e trigger word releases the entire turn, including a message that merely discusses the word. This is

on purpose: ambiguity is resolved by what the user typed, not by the plugin guessing intent.
4. **C
ommand judgement is a name comparison, not a parser.** `Get-ChildItem $p.GetFiles()` is counted as p
ersistent, because the plugin does not evaluate the pipeline. The error direction is chosen: over-co

unt, never under-count.
5. **A tool call is one count**, regardless of how many files it touches.
### Why not X
| Alternative | Why not |
| **Hard-block instead of counting** | Tried first in an OpenClaw build. A wall turns every write in
to an interruption the user did not ask for. With a counter and an explicit stop instruction, the mo
del does the arithmetic itself — it stopped at 11/15 on its own. The brake works better than the wal

l. |
| **Plugin-only, no DSH host hooks** | The per-turn count has to come from the **tool-dispatch
layer**. A wrapper around the model API cannot see individual tool calls, so it cannot count them. T

he count lives where the calls live. |
| **Fold it into the sandbox** | Different question, differen
t layer. A sandbox answers "is this allowed?". This answers "how much has happened?". Sitting inside
the sandbox would tie a budget to a permission model that changes underneath it. |
## 3. What this framework lets you tune
**Everything is configurable; nothing is hard-coded.** Configuration lives in the profile's `cordis.
g is configurable; nothing is hard-coded.** Configuration lives in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`.
## 4. What counts as a "persistent operation"
The test: **after the action completes, has the outside world changed?**

### Limitations
- **Requires the channel plugin to provide the `wechatQueue` service.** Without it the guard degrade

s to not blocking, and this plugin will not error.
- **Only the service name `wechatQueue` is recogn
ised.** Other channels (Slack, Discord, …) need their own same-named service, or a branch added here

.
- **WeChat will never have clickable options.** That is an inherent cost of a turn-based channel,
not something this plugin can work around.
